是的，我们目前有六个人，所以是一个相当小型的团队。我觉得招聘这件事挺有意思的，你看网上那么多招聘建议，看完后总觉得“这太显而易见了”。但当你亲身经历时，才会突然意识到“原来人们说这些话是有道理的”。举几个简单的例子：真正难找的人，是那种对工作充满热情、愿意付出额外20%努力的人。特别是招聘初创公司的人（这里不针对具体公司），他们往往期望一份年薪40万美元的工作，按固定工时上班，完成代码后就下班——这基本上是大公司员工习惯的模式。但当你把这种标准应用到小型初创公司时，挑战就来了。初创公司的成功很大程度上取决于每个人的自驱力：比如“不，我今晚必须加班完成任务，而不是走走形式”，以及“我要为公司的目标全力以赴，而不是只完成任务”。这些道理听起来显而易见，但当你真正感受到那种只求完成任务的人和真正有使命感的人之间的差别时，那种差别就非常明显了。对前20名员工来说，这至关重要。招聘这些人没有标准答案，不能在招聘说明里写上“重视结果”然后就等着申请人蜂拥而至。

接下来要考虑的是，如何筛选出这些人？这时候使命契合度就显得至关重要了。你必须找到那些对你的事业有额外私人关怀的人。比如Palantir就雇佣了许多退伍军人，或者比普通科技员工更有爱国情怀的人，这些人对Palantir有额外动力。对我来说，医疗健康领域的招聘更讲究。比如有亲属曾经历癌症等疾病的人，他们会更有动力去关心你所做的事业，并付出更多努力。因此，早期筛选时要聚焦使命契合度，比如“你曾为达成目标付出多大努力，为什么？”。这样的问题能区分出不同的人群，很多人都答不上来。这就是我最大的收获：招聘不只是测试技能，固然重要，但更关键的是寻找那额外20%的努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting, everything you've shared is essentially around motivation, and drive, and passion, and kind of just commitment to working on this intently, and it's almost like a second thought of just like, oh, also they're really smart and skilled at stuff. It feels like that's just table stakes and this is actually what makes the difference in your experience.
turns.zh: 太有意思了，你分享的这些内容基本上都围绕着动机、驱动力和激情展开，还有全身心投入工作的决心。而人们往往会把这些视为理所当然，认为这不过是成功的必要条件。但实际上，这些品质才是真正让你的经历与众不同的地方。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yeah, I totally agree, and I think it's different for every business. So I think if you're in a space like B2B SaaS where maybe it's a little harder to tell the story of like, oh, this is so mission-critical, whatever, there are other ways of getting at this thing. So for example, I know a lot of people, again, it's a little played out now, but I know a lot of people who for sales teams, they will explicitly go for people who were professional athletes or played sports in college, and it's like, okay, what does that test for? It's like you are very, very disciplined, you're very, very goals and numbers oriented and you're willing to just work really, really hard. And so there's all these kind of lateral ways of getting at these qualities that I think you just have to be intentional about as a founder. As a personal example, I'm a runner and so I actually love meeting fellow runners and I kind of joke like, "Oh, maybe I'll go higher from run clubs or something like that." (01:03:57): But it's just same with I play a lot of chess, I love meeting chess players. I'm not necessarily saying that's the right kind of hire for me, but I think having this thing of here are some traits that seem uncorrelated, but which actually give you good signal to this person's personality, those are actually really important. The last thing I'll say just as a funny illustration of that concept is I think Max Levchin tells the story of somebody interviewing at PayPal early on and he passed all the skill interviews and then it just got to the final round and he said something about liking to shoot hoops, like he liked to play basketball, and they were like instant reject. The vibe here was like if you're not a mega Linux nerd, hardcore computer person, then we don't want you here, even if you actually passed all the tests just because you like to shoot hoops. Now whether that was the right call or the wrong call, don't know, but that's an example of what I'm talking about.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全同意你的观点。我认为每个行业的情况都不尽相同。比如，在B2B SaaS领域，要想讲述一个“这项任务至关重要”之类的故事可能更困难，但总有其他方法能传达同样的理念。举个例子，我认识很多人，虽然这个方法现在已经有点老生常谈了，但他们在组建销售团队时，会明确倾向于选择有专业运动员背景或大学运动员经历的人。这背后传递的是什么信息呢？这意味着他们极其自律，目标和数据导向，并且愿意付出巨大努力。还有很多类似的迂回方式能挖掘出这些品质，作为创始人，你必须有意识地去发掘这些特质。以我个人为例，我是个跑步爱好者，所以我特别喜欢结交其他跑者，还会开玩笑说：“或许我该从跑步俱乐部招人之类的。” （01:03:57）但道理是一样的，我也经常下棋，喜欢结交棋友。虽然我不认为这些人一定适合我公司，但我认为有些看似无关的特质能有效传递出对方的性格特征，这确实很重要。最后我再举个有趣的例子说明这个观点。我记得Max Levchin讲过一个故事，早期PayPal面试时，有个候选人通过了所有技能测试，但到了最后一轮面试时，他提到自己喜欢打篮球，结果被当场拒绝。当时的氛围是，如果你不是个超级Linux极客、深度技术宅，那我们就不需要你，就算你通过了所有测试，只要你喜欢打篮球，我们也不想要你。虽然这做法对错尚有争议，但这正是我要说明的点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a great echo back. People hearing this may be like, "What the hell? How dare they do that?" But this is exactly what you said at the beginning of our conversation, that like an approach to building a generational business is to be very clear about who this is not for, and that's okay, it's your company, not everyone needs to work there. And it's almost saving them time because they might realize this isn't for me, this isn't the people I want to be around necessarily. So I think it's important to see that side of it, is it's your business, it's important to be clear about who is a good fit for the company and who's not. Speaking of that, let's talk about product management for a bit. I know Palantir PMs are not traditional product managers. I imagine people have the title, Product Manager at Palantir, okay, so if so, as far as you understand what's the difference between say a PM at Palantir versus a traditional PM say at a FANG company?
turns.zh: 我觉得你总结得太到位了。听众可能觉得：“什么鬼？他们怎么能这么做？” 但这正是你开场时说的，打造代际企业的关键在于明确“这份工作不适合谁”，这没关系，这是你的公司，不需要所有人都来工作。这甚至能节省他们的时间，让他们意识到这份工作不适合自己，不必浪费时间纠结。说到这里，咱们再聊聊产品管理。我知道Palantir的产品经理和传统产品经理不同。我猜Palantir的产品经理头衔是产品经理，但据我了解，Palantir的产品经理和FANG公司（Facebook、亚马逊、谷歌、网飞）的产品经理有何不同？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: The big difference or one big difference I noticed was that they were extremely careful about only making people PMs who had first proven themselves out as forward deploying engineers. You basically could not become a PM any other way. So as an example, when I mentioned earlier the thing that we built for the plane factory, the person who was managing that deployment, she later became the PM for ontology, and it was just because she'd kind of proven her method in the field. And the reason for that's pretty simple, it's going to be someone who understand how customers work and has that customer empathy, and it's going to be someone who has this drive to get things done because that's what BD selected for. I think the failure mode that they were very, very averse to in traditional PMs was this kind of Google Docs syndrome of like, okay, I'm going to write my product requirement documents, and I'm going to manage it in this very sort of sane, rational way I think, so the company was really rigorous about that. (01:07:04): And so basically PMs were almost always internal promotions and they always came from BD. I am not aware of a single case where we took somebody who was a PM at a place like Google, which produces many excellent PMs and hired them successfully into Palantir, it's just a very different vibe. So I think that was one thing. This is maybe more of a classic PM trait, but you just had to be either an engineer yourself or extremely good at working with engineers, and the ones I saw who succeeded the most were just best friends with their engineering team. And the team would always just be like one, it was called the group pm and then it would be a lot of very, very good engineers. And basically the success or failure mode was just do the engineers and trust you? I mentioned before Palantir how is very almost disagreeable personalities, and so if you didn't gain the trust of engineering team pretty fast, you didn't last very long.
turns.zh: 我注意到的一个重大区别，或者说一个关键区别在于，他们极其谨慎，只让那些先在一线工程岗位上证明了自己的人担任产品经理。除此之外，几乎没有其他晋升途径。举个例子，我之前提到的我们为飞机工厂开发的项目，那位负责该项目部署的工程师后来成为了本体论部门的产品经理，原因很简单——她在实战中证明了自己的方法论。这一决策背后的逻辑很简单：产品经理必须理解客户的运作方式，具备客户同理心，并且要有推动项目落地的驱动力——毕竟Palantir的BD部门正是为此而选拔人才的。他们极其反感传统产品经理身上那种Google Docs式的思维模式，比如“好的，我要写产品需求文档，然后用一种理性、合理的方式管理它”。公司对此要求非常严格。（01:07:04）：因此，产品经理基本上都是内部晋升，而且都来自BD部门。我不知道有哪一个案例是我们从谷歌这样的培养了许多优秀产品经理的公司成功挖来的。这里氛围截然不同。所以这就是关键点之一。这或许更符合经典的产品经理特质，但你必须要么自己是工程师，要么非常善于与工程师合作。我见过最成功的产品经理都是与工程团队关系极为融洽的。团队通常只有一位PM，叫做“组内PM”，成员都是非常优秀的工程师。成功或失败的关键在于能否赢得工程团队的信任？我之前提到过，Palantir的员工个性极具挑战性。如果你不能迅速获得工程团队的信任，就很难长久待下去。

turns.zh: 我认为我们已经解答了为什么Palantir的产品经理如此成功这个问题。首先，招聘标准基本上是从多个角度筛选领导者，比如那些与创始人共同解决实际问题，打造能盈利的产品的人，这些人才最终成为Palantir的产品经理，之后有的离职创业，有的成为其他公司的首席产品官。

turns.zh: 是啊，这确实太疯狂了。我在Palantir的一个小团队里工作，刚加入时团队规模约20到25人，现在这25个人中至少有6位要么是独角兽公司创始人，要么是即将成为独角兽的创始人——这个比例实在太高了。还有更多人最近在更早期阶段就成为了创业者。所以确实存在很多卓越的小群体，看到这些真是很有趣。我觉得另一个推动因素是，当你离开Palantir时，这家公司实在太有吸引力了，以至于它的员工留存率非常高——人们往往会比硅谷平均任职时间长得多。所以当你离开时，往往是出于某种特定原因，比如想挑战更高的职业境界。很少有人离开Palantir后会去传统科技公司工作。要么就是去创业，要么就是留在Palantir。听起来有点像邪教，但大家都这么想。

turns.zh: 我完全能理解这种现象。很多离开Airbnb的人都没能找到更有意义的事业，实在太难了，尤其是在早期阶段。有一个很有趣的数据，我之前没分享过——当你观察YC的创始人来自哪里时，你可能在帖子里提到过，YC的Palantir前创始人比Google前创始人还多，而Google的规模可是Palantir的50倍左右。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yeah, it's a really interesting topic, it's definitely very nuanced. I think what I was trying to say in that post was a couple of things. One was that there was a lot of upside there. So I worked on the US Covid response, I have friends who worked on Operation Warp Speed, and these are all things that I think saved a lot of lives, and I was pretty focused while I was working at NIH on cancer research. And so to me, these were just obviously good things and you couldn't do them anywhere else, and so that was alone a reason to stay. The question I had in that post was, well, okay, there are definitely going to be other pieces of this that people object to. So during the 2016 to 2020 era, it became a pretty common thing to go into work in New York and you'd have people protesting outside your office or doing all kinds of things. And so there was this question of, well, is this okay? And I think the point I was trying to make was it's rare that disengagement is the correct answer, and I think it's more recognized now, but especially then it went a bit too far. (01:11:41): So the famous example here is Google kind of disengaging with a Pentagon AI project just because some people felt that working with the Pentagon was itself morally bad. I think that's a way to sort of the left of what the median American would say, I think the median American would say it's fine to work on defense stuff within reason and assuming you're doing largely good things, and so there was just this kind of almost arbitrage there at some point of just hang on, it's not like working on defense is inherently evil, it's actually a pretty interesting thing. And then there's this question of, well, would you rather be in the room and making this better or not? And so I'm struggling with how much I can share here, but as a simple example, if you're doing even a workflow, which I think many people would not be super comfortable with, let's say you're targeting somebody for some kind of strike. If you compare the way it's done now to maybe the way it was done in 2010, it's going to be a lot more targeted, it's going to be a lot more accurate, and so you've actually improved that process and reduced the chance of error. Maybe you should feel good about that, right? Now, that is a bullet many people are not willing to bite. (01:12:52): I didn't work on the defense side of the company myself, but I think you have to be okay with these kinds of grade zones and actually actively thinking about what you are doing. And that doesn't mean that it's always the right thing to do to work in a defense company. Maybe we go into a very dark future and we start being the bad guys in some ways, and then it's probably not a great idea to work at a defense company. So it's a shifting landscape but I kind of felt pretty strongly that a lot of people in tech just didn't want to think about this at all. (01:13:29): So you have engineers now who are working on optimizing short form videos for higher engagement, and you sort of want to say to them like, "Hey, are you thinking about what this is doing to the brains of young children?" Or "Have you seen an 11-year-old kind of scrolling something for five hours and do you think this is a good thing?" And I think people don't want to think about this stuff too much. I'm not saying I know the answer, but there was almost this refusal to look at what tech was doing from a political lens for a very long time. It was just like, "Hey, let us play with our toys, let us sit in our little park, and don't bother us, and we're just going to build cool stuff and launch it." (01:14:08): And 2025, we're in a very, very different state of the world, tech is involved in politics now, and politics basically came to tech. There's this famous image of Mark Zuckerberg, he's sitting in Congress and he kind of looks very pale, and he's like, "Why have they dragged me in here again?" But I think tech went through this journey of, oh, we're suddenly becoming important now, oh, we're really, really important now, oh, we better stop playing this game of politics. And so I think what I'm saying now is a lot more consensus than it was 10 years ago, but at the time, the feeling was just like, "Look what we are doing is political, so you better engage with that."
turns.zh:
是啊，这确实是个很有趣的话题，而且涉及诸多复杂层面。我在那篇帖子里想表达的观点有几个方面。首先，美国在新冠疫情期间的应对措施确实有很多积极成果。比如，我参与过美国新冠疫情应对工作，还有朋友参与过“快速行动计划”，所有这些努力都拯救了无数生命。我在国家卫生研究院（NIH）专注癌症研究期间，也觉得自己的工作意义重大——这些显然都是积极正面的，而且这些工作在其他地方是无法开展的，这本身就是我留下的理由。但帖子中我也提到了一个问题：人们对某些事务的反对意见确实存在。在2016至2020年间，去纽约上班经常会遇到人们在办公室外抗议，这让我不禁思考——这种行为是否合理？我认为答案是，逃避责任绝非明智之举。虽然如今人们对此的认识有所提升，但当时这种极端做法实在过火了。（01:11:41）举个著名的例子：谷歌因为部分员工认为与五角大楼合作本质上不道德而退出五角大楼的人工智能项目。这类观点其实偏离了大多数美国人的立场。大多数美国人认为，在合理范围内参与国防项目并无不可，只要所做之事本质上是善意的。所以在某种程度上，人们会权衡利弊——留下来工作是否比逃避现实更有意义？我难以在此详细阐述，但举个简单的例子：就连许多人可能不愿触及的流程，比如针对特定目标实施打击行动。对比2010年与现在的执行方式，后者显然更具精准性和针对性，极大降低了误伤风险。这难道不值得欣慰吗？但这类观点在许多人眼中依然难以接受。

（01:12:52）我本人并未在国防部门工作，但我认为必须正视这些道德灰色地带，主动审视自己的行为。这并不意味着在国防公司工作永远正确。若未来世界陷入黑暗局面，我们或许会成为反派角色，那时选择国防公司或许就不明智了。不过大环境确实在变化，我深切感受到许多科技从业者根本不愿深思这些问题。（01:13:29）比如，现在有工程师致力于优化短视频以提高用户参与度，你想对他们说：「嘿，你们有没有考虑过这对儿童大脑的影响？」或者「你见过11岁孩子连续五小时刷短视频吗？你觉得这正常吗？」但人们往往不愿深究这些问题。当然我也不自诩能给出完美答案，但长期以来，人们始终拒绝从政治视角审视科技行业的运作，仿佛只要埋头搞技术就万事大吉。
并将其推向市场。  
（01:14:08）：到2025年，世界局势将截然不同。科技如今已深度介入政治领域，而政治力量也已渗透至科技行业。马克·扎克伯格在国会听证会上的画面令人难忘——他面色苍白，似乎在想：“他们怎么又把我请来了？” 但我认为科技行业曾经历过这样一个阶段：起初我们突然意识到自己变得举足轻重，接着又认为自己至关重要，最后不得不停止玩弄政治游戏。如今我所说的观点，比十年前已更具共识性。但在当时，人们的普遍态度是：“我们所做的一切都具有政治属性，所以你们最好参与其中。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think when this became really real for a lot of people is with the Ukraine War, the government's running out of certain vehicles and ammunition, we're just not able to produce it, and then we're like, "Oh, thank God for a company like Anduril and all these other tech companies that are actually ahead and keeping us ahead." I think the only reason the US is ahead of that...
turns.zh: 我认为对很多人来说，乌克兰战争才是让这一切真正成为现实的转折点。政府的某些车辆和弹药库存告急，我们根本无力生产，随后人们感慨道："感谢上帝，有安德里尔这样的公司，还有其他诸多科技企业，他们始终走在前沿，助力我们保持领先。" 我觉得美国之所以能在太空竞赛中领先中国，唯一的原因就是SpaceX这样的公司长期深耕该领域。因此，许多人逐渐意识到，或许我们确实需要这些技术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And keeping us ahead. I think the only reason the US is ahead of China and the space race is because SpaceX just is one company that just has been doing this for a long time. So I think a lot of people have kind of realized, okay, maybe we need these things.
turns.zh: 并保持领先地位。我认为美国能在太空竞赛中领先中国，唯一的原因就是SpaceX这样的公司长期深耕该领域。因此，许多人逐渐意识到，或许我们确实需要这些技术。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Right. And I would make this argument as well, it's like people are like, well, how can you feel good about working in defense? And it's like, well, you're not going to feel great if China invades Taiwan, actually, you're not going to. I think you are probably also not going to like that outcome. So we do just live in this world where you do need to build up deterrents to these things and they better be good. So to me, it didn't feel that difficult of a question. I think when you zoom into particular things, they can be very difficult questions and there have been a bunch of those in the last couple of years. But yeah, again, disengagement isn't the answer.
turns.zh: 好的。我也想谈谈这个问题。有些人会问：在国防领域工作怎么能让人感到自豪呢？对此我要说，如果中国入侵台湾，你肯定不会感到开心。你大概也不会乐见这种结果。所以我们确实生活在这样一个世界里——你必须建立对这些威胁的威慑力量，而且这些防御体系必须足够强大。对我来说，这个问题并不难理解。当然，当你深入探讨具体问题时，可能会遇到非常棘手的难题，过去几年里就有很多这样的例子。不过，退出国际事务绝不是解决之道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And again, it's not for everyone. I think that's an important kind of theme through this conversation is some companies ... like, to build ... sometimes to build a generational, really successful company, you need to turn some people off because that's what brings in the best talent oftentimes. (01:16:03): Okay. Just a few more questions. Kind of like stepping back a little bit. You're building a company again. What are a few core pieces of advice that you're bringing to your new startup that will inform how you build this company, from your experience at Palantir? We talked about a lot of stuff. Is there anything, I don't know if there are three things that you think are like, "I'm definitely going to do these things this way because it worked really well at Palantir."
turns.zh: 是的。再说一次，这并不适合所有人。我认为这次对话中一个重要的主题是，有些公司……比如，要建立……有时候要打造一家经久不衰、真正成功的公司，你就得得罪一些人——因为这往往能吸引最优秀的人才。（01:16:03）：好的，再问几个问题。先退后一步。你现在又在创业了。从你在Palantir的经验中，有哪些核心建议会影响你新公司的建设？我们讨论了很多内容。是否有哪三点是你认为“在Palantir行之有效，所以我一定要在新公司这样做”的？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: One thing is probably just really fast iteration cycles. So placing a lot of bets and then being really rigorous about just going through that cycle very soon. I have this [inaudible 01:16:40]principles, and one of the things on there is basically saying EOP successes goes up the more bets you make, and it's sort of a function of how many bets you make and the probability of success of those individual bets, right? And so one easy way to almost guarantee that you'll hit something is just to make a lot of bets and then just kind of cycle through them very quickly. Now, obviously this is difficult, often this question of, well, is this bet actually failing or are we quitting too soon, kind of thing. But that's kind of one principle I take, is just test this thing very early. You know, like the classic "why feed, why see" thing is just when you take something to a customer, ask them to pay you a lot of money and [inaudible 01:17:22] then find a new problem. Don't wait three weeks, which is what every founding team typically does because you don't have that kind of time. (01:17:29): I do think the importance of just having a really tight, distinctive internal culture and building a strong feeling of trust within a team is really important. And kind of like you mentioned with Airbnb, and people definitely felt this at Palantir, there was this feeling of like, well, you worked here, you must be good. I trust you, and all of that. And I think it's so important to create that and you kind of know that feeling. That's what ... like, people ask me, should I go work at place X or should I just go be a founder straightaway? I don't know the answer for everyone, but I will say one of the benefits of working at a place like that is you just have all these internal benchmarks now for, okay, this is what this should feel like, and if it doesn't feel like that, we're off. And I can't imagine not having those benchmarks and just kind of having to figure it all out. (01:18:21): So yeah, I think that thing, too, is just distinctive, internal, strong team culture. And then I think for me, think three is just working with a really messy part of the real world. So I kind of joked when I left, like, I am excited to just do pure software. I'm excited to, I don't know, I want to build an ID or something and just not have a support email even and all of that. But it turned out, look, my comparative advantage in a lot of ways was the networks I'd built and the experience I'd had in engaging with the messy parts of the world. And they do need technology a lot, right? (01:19:00): There's this horrifying thought I have sometimes of just like, maybe we'll get ATI in the next two years and the healthcare sector will still be broken and it will still be impossible to afford rent in New York City and build houses and all these things. And that may well become true. And so I think it's important to engage with those parts of the world too, even though they're really, really challenging. And I think the really nice thing about LLMs is that actually, there's so many workflows now that are accessible to you as a tech founder and people are somehow more open to working with tech companies than they ever were before. Selling into the sectors of the economy in 2015, incredibly hard. I think now post the ChatGPT moment, people are willing to give chances to small startups that they weren't willing to do previously. As you mentioned earlier, the cost of doing things like forward-deployed engineering has fallen by maybe five to 10 x now at least. And so there's a lot of new possibilities and I'm excited to engage with the best.
turns.zh:
或许最重要的一点是快速的迭代周期。因此，我们会频繁尝试新想法，然后迅速完成整个迭代周期。我有一些[听不清01:16:40]原则，其中一条基本观点是，EOP（工程到产品）的成功概率会随着尝试次数的增加而提升，这取决于尝试次数和每个尝试的成功概率。那么，要想几乎确定能有所收获，最简单的方法就是频繁尝试并快速迭代。当然，问题往往在于判断某个尝试是否真的失败了，还是我们过早放弃了。但我秉持的一个原则是，尽早测试新想法。就像经典的“为什么喂食，为什么验证”原则，当你把产品推向客户、收取高额费用后，却发现新的问题。这时候不要等三周——毕竟大多数创业团队都等不了那么久。（01:17:29）我认为打造紧密独特的内部文化、在团队中建立牢固的信任感至关重要。正如你提到的Airbnb案例，Palantir的员工也深有体会——在这里工作的人都会被默认是优秀的，彼此信任。这种文化的塑造非常重要，你能感受到那种氛围。当有人问我应该去X公司工作还是直接创业时，我无法给出统一答案，但我要说，在这种公司工作的好处之一就是，你能内置一套标准来衡量是否达标，如果达不到标准，就果断调整。我无法想象没有这些标准只能靠自己摸索。（01:18:21）还有一点是与真实世界复杂场景的深度对接。比如我离开Palantir时曾开玩笑说，很期待做纯软件开发，比如开发个ID系统之类的，甚至不需要客服邮箱。但后来发现，我的比较优势其实在于我建立的人脉网络和与现实世界复杂场景打交道的经验。这些领域对技术的需求同样巨大啊。（01:19:00）有时我会产生可怕的担忧：也许未来两年内我们就能掌握AIGC技术，但医疗保健系统依然崩坏，纽约市的房租依然高得离谱，房屋建设依然停滞。这种情况很可能成真。因此，尽管与现实世界的交融充满挑战，但我们仍需积极参与其中。LLM技术的出现确实为科技创业者带来了新机遇，人们对与科技公司的合作也比以往开放得多。2015年想把技术卖给传统行业难如登天，现在ChatGPT引发的热潮让人们更愿意给小型初创公司机会。正如你之前提到的，前端工程的成本现在至少降低了5到10倍。总之，机遇比比皆是。
种种可能性让我倍感兴奋，我渴望与最优秀的人才携手共进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is some alpha right there that you're finding, that some of these very large organizations are more open to working with startups, because classically, investors don't want to invest in companies that are going after healthcare companies and governments and things like that. So it is really interesting actually to hear. (01:20:17): I'm going to mirror back the tips you just shared, and there's actually a secondary tip that I think is the more interesting piece. So the first thing you're taking away is iterate quickly, but I love your tip of ask for lots of money quickly, early, to see if it's an actual idea that people will pay lots of money for. And if not, move on. I love that. (01:20:35): The other is build a very distinct culture, but the piece you share there that I love even more is this idea of knowing what a high bar looks like, knowing what awesome A plus people look like, and you need to work at a company like Palantir to actually see that. So the advice there I feel is just work at a company that is amazing, first, with the best talent, to understand what that should look like, plus you build a network of those folks. So I think that's really interesting. (01:21:03): And then the other pieces of advice you're pulling away is work on really hard, messy problems because that's where the biggest opportunities are, and it's sounding like this is the easiest time to actually do that. Amazing. (01:21:13): Okay. I'm going to take us to a recurring theme on this podcast called AI Corner. And what we do in AI Corner is we share some way that .. and this is you sharing ... some way that you've found AI to be useful in your day- to-day, either in life or in work. Is there any way you found some tool ... some AI tool useful that you can share?
turns.zh: 哇，你发现的这个机会真是了不起啊！现在很多大型机构都更愿意与初创企业合作，因为传统上，投资者不愿投资那些针对医疗保健公司、政府等领域的公司。所以能听到你分享这些真的很令人兴奋。（01:20:17）：我要回顾一下你刚才提到的建议，还有一个更让我感兴趣的次要建议。首先，你提到的要快速迭代，但我特别喜欢你提到的尽早、大量筹集资金的建议，这样就能知道是否有市场愿意为这个创意买单。如果不行，就及时调整方向。我觉得这个方法很棒。（01:20:35）：另一个建议是建立独特的企业文化，但我更欣赏你提到的要清楚高标准的样子，知道A+级人才该是什么样子。这只有在像Palantir这样的公司才能亲眼见识到。所以我的建议是，先在一家顶尖公司工作，接触最优秀的人才，了解行业标杆的样子，同时建立人脉网络。我觉得这真的很有意义。（01:21:03）：还有一个建议是解决那些复杂、混乱的问题，因为这些地方往往蕴藏着最大的机遇。听起来现在正是尝试的好时机。太棒了。（01:21:13）：好的，我要带大家进入本期播客的常规环节——“AI角落”。在“AI角落”，我们会分享AI技术在日常生活或工作中发挥作用的案例。你们有没有发现什么AI工具特别实用的，可以和大家分享一下？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Oh my gosh, there are so many. I'll give you a few examples. So I use Wispr Flow quite a bit. So this is the talk to your keyboard and it will transcribe for you app. Very good. It's just great when you are iterating very quickly with an LLM and sometimes you have to do these paragraph-long prompts and it's just easier to speak into them. So Wispr Flow, I like.
turns.zh: 天哪，太多了。我举几个例子吧。比如我经常用Wispr Flow。这是一款语音转文字的应用。非常好用。当你和大语言模型快速迭代时，经常需要写长段落的提示语，用语音输入会更方便。所以我很喜欢Wispr Flow。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to double down on that, you press a button and you start talking-
turns.zh: 再详细说一下，按个按钮就能开始说话——

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's writing out what you're saying. Cool. And there have been these products for a long time, Dragon Dictate and all these guys. Is the difference now these are just very, very good now at actually transcribing what you're saying?
turns.zh: 它会把你说的话转写出来。太酷了。类似的产品已经存在很久了，比如Dragon Dictate之类的。现在的区别在于这些应用在转写语音方面做得非常好了？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: I think that's right. Yeah, they use a really good model and so it rarely makes mistakes even when I think it's quite challenging. And then, yeah, the UX I think they just nailed. So that's really good one. (01:22:27): I love Claude Code for developing. Even though I have my complaints about it, there's something just very addictive about just telling it what to do. And it's basically something that you run within the terminal of your computer, and so you just type Claude, it opens up the Claude interface. It's very cute, it's very beautifully designed, and you just tell it what to do. And it actually operates on the file system directly. So if you're like, "Hey, create a bunch of these files," that'll just do it and you don't need to go and muck around inside Finder yourself. And then it'll do these really complicated pull requests and it'll basically execute them quite well. So to me, this is a very exciting kind of preview of AI agents.
turns.zh: 我觉得没错。是啊，他们用了一个非常好的模型，所以即使我觉得这很具挑战性，它也很少出错。然后，我觉得他们的用户体验设计得非常棒。这真是很棒的产品。（01:22:27）：我喜欢Claude Code用于开发。尽管我对它也有不满的地方，但只要告诉它该怎么做，就会有一种让人上瘾的感觉。基本上，你只需在电脑终端中运行Claude，输入“Claude”就能打开Claude界面。它设计得非常可爱、美观，你只需告诉它该做什么。它实际上直接操作文件系统。比如，如果你说：“嘿，创建一堆这些文件”，它就会直接处理，不需要你自己在Finder里费劲操作。它还能处理非常复杂的拉取请求，并且能很好地执行这些操作。所以对我来说，这是一个非常令人兴奋的AI代理预览。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's what I was going to ask. So this is essentially an AI agent engineer. I didn't know that's what Claude Code did. Very cool.
turns.zh: 这正是我想问的。所以这本质上是一个AI代理工程师。我之前都不知道Claude Code有这个功能。太酷了。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yeah. It's sort of a guided agent, but yeah, it is really sweet. And then yeah, I'm just enjoying ... you know, every week there's a new, wonderful new thing to play with. Last seven days, I've been testing Gemini Pro 2.5. Excellent model. I don't love Google's UX sometimes, but I was playing with that. And I use LLMs every day for all kinds of things. The other day I was doing taxes and I needed to classify a bunch of transactions based on some metadata, and so I just wrote a script up really quickly and it did that. So.
turns.zh: 是啊。这有点像一个引导式代理，不过确实很棒。然后我现在就很享受……你知道的，每周都有新的好玩的东西可以尝试。过去七天，我一直在测试Gemini Pro 2.5。模型很棒。我有时不太喜欢谷歌的用户体验，但我一直在试用它。我每天都在用LLMs做各种事情。前几天我在报税，需要根据一些元数据对一堆交易进行分类，所以我很快写了个脚本，然后它就完成了。所以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just the smile on your face as you're describing all these AI tools. I think a lot of people are just like, holy shit, I'm just overwhelmed with all the things I need to be paying attention to. All these things I'm hearing, all these tools I got to try. And I love just this vibe of just like, this is incredible and so fun. We need more of that. (01:24:01): Okay. I'm going to take us to another recurring segment on the podcast. You're going to get a double whammy. Contrarian Corner. So here's the question. What's something that you believe that most other people don't?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你描述这些AI工具时脸上的笑容。我觉得很多人都觉得，天哪，所有需要关注的东西都太多了。听到的所有这些东西，所有需要尝试的工具。我就喜欢这种感觉，觉得这太不可思议、太有趣了。我们需要更多这样的东西。（01:24:01）：好的，我要把节目带入另一个固定环节了。你们将迎来双重惊喜。异见角。那么问题来了。有什么是你认为大多数人都不认同的观点？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: I think going to college is great. I think this is a somewhat contrarian view within tech, maybe not in the broader economy, but I often see people saying just like, oh, if you can just drop out when you're 18 and just start working, why would you go to college? And I think this is completely wrong, but maybe it's good advice for 5% of the population who probably would've been to your fellows anyway. But college is one of the few times when you can just make really, really deep friendships. You are in typically a nice campus. If you're in North America, you get to spend all of your time just thinking and writing papers and reading books and hanging out with your friends. (01:24:49): And it's actually very precious and it's very hard to find that kind of time after you turn 21 because you got to pay your rent, you've got to work, you've got to do all this stuff. Let's say you make a bunch of money, you take a career break, it's still ... all your friends are working and you always feel like there's a ticking time or on top of your head or something. (01:25:09): So just taking those three or four years at the very beginning and going really deep on lots of different intellectual topics and being able to try different things and discover more about yourself. I'm a big college fan. I can't comment on the ROI or whatever. I personally think the ROI is great, even though the fees are kind of high in the U.S., but that's probably my kind of contrarian within tech view is don't drop out of college unless you have a really good reason.
turns.zh: 我认为上大学很棒。我觉得这在科技界算是个非主流观点，也许在更广泛的经济领域不算，但我经常看到人们说类似"如果你18岁就能退学去工作，干嘛还要上大学？"之类的话。我觉得这种观点完全错误，不过对5%的人来说或许是个好建议——反正他们可能本来就会去读大学。但大学是为数不多的能让你结交真正深厚友谊的时期。你身处优美的校园环境中。若是在北美，你可以把所有时间都花在思考、写论文、阅读书籍以及和朋友们相聚上。（01:24:49）这种时光其实非常珍贵，而过了21岁就很难再找到这样的时光了——因为你得付房租、工作、处理各种事务。即便你赚了大钱、休假，也总会觉得时间紧迫，压力重重。（01:25:09）所以在刚开始的三四年里，能深入探讨各种知识主题、尝试不同事物、更好地认识自己，这真是太棒了。我非常推崇大学教育。我暂且不谈投资回报率之类的，我个人认为即便美国学费高昂，投资回报率也是很可观的。但这或许就是我这个科技界的非主流观点吧——除非有充分理由，否则别退学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny that that is contrarian and it does sound contrarian. I had a great time in college here. Here. Okay. Is there anything else, Nabeel, that you wanted to share or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 真有趣，这观点确实算非主流。我在大学里过得很开心。嗯。好的。Nabeel，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享或留给他们的吗？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: No, I think it's a really exciting time in the world. I think AI can be exhausting, but it does really just open up the possibility of building a better world in all these ways. And so I think just reassess what you're doing every couple of months and make sure that it's aligned with where I think AI is going and make sure that you are working on something that you feel has very high potential if it succeeds. And I think that's more important than ever now just because the amount of leverage we have with technology is at the highest point in history.
turns.zh: 没有了。我觉得当下世界形势令人振奋。人工智能确实让人筋疲力尽，但它确实为我们开辟了构建更美好世界的可能性。所以我认为每隔几个月就重新评估自己的工作方向很重要，确保它与我对人工智能发展方向的看法相契合，确保自己正在做的事情一旦成功就具有极高的潜力。在当下，这比以往任何时候都更加重要，因为我们借助科技所能发挥的影响力达到了历史顶峰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me double click on that real quick. So for people that want to do what you're describing, what helps you understand where AI is heading and just kind of align with it, are there places of information and news you find useful? Is it just play with it kind of thing? What would you recommend?
turns.zh: 让我再快速点一下。如果有人想做你描述的那些事，有助于他们理解人工智能发展方向并与之保持一致的信息和新闻来源有哪些？是说多玩玩技术吗？你有什么推荐？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: This is the big question. I use X a lot to keep on top of AI, so I would just recommend finding a good Twitter list and maybe following people off of that. There's some good newsletters. I really like Latent Space, I know his X handle, it's Swyx, S-W-Y-X. I can't remember his actual name, but that one is very good and it's pretty technical. I would recommend trying to stick to the more technical newsletters if possible. I think there's a lot of philosophy about AI or AI policy type stuff, and I think that's good if that's your area, but it's an area where it's very easy to have a lot of takes on it. You're not necessarily learning a lot by reading those. (01:27:16): But I think it's just important to know what's going on and make sure you are revisiting your own workflows as often as possible. And just making sure that the people who went here are going to be the kind of hybrid cyborgs who fuse with the AIs. This actually played out in chess, if I can take a slight detour, is the chess players who succeeded the most in the mid 2010s especially were the ones who were really early adopters of neural network based chess engines. So when DeepMind did that thing, there was very quickly an open source version of it called Leela, and you find basically the very top players like Magnus Carlson, Fabiano, they were the ones who kind of mind melded the most with Leela and learned how it played and then kind of started copying its moves. (01:28:06): And so I think just becoming a cyborg to the extent that you can. And then I think there's this barbell thing of, it's also important to just leave everything at go touch grass just for your own mental sanity.
turns.zh:
这是个关键问题。我经常用X平台来追踪AI领域动态，所以我建议你先找一个优质的Twitter账号列表，或许从其中的人物入手追踪。市面上有不少优质的订阅资讯，我个人很推荐《Latent Space》（推特账号：Swyx，S-W-Y-X）。我记不清他的真名了，但这个账号内容非常专业，技术性极强。如果可能的话，我建议大家尽量关注技术性较强的资讯推送。市面上有很多关于AI哲学或政策的讨论内容，如果这正是你的研究方向，那固然不错，但这类内容往往众说纷纭，读者很难从中获得实质性收获。  

（01:27:16）不过，我认为最重要的是了解行业动态，并尽可能频繁地审视自己的工作流程。正如我之前提到的，确保自己能成为与AI深度融合的混合体。这在国际象棋领域已有先例——2010年代中期，那些在国际象棋领域取得显著成就的顶尖棋手，多是率先采用神经网络引擎的先行者。例如，当DeepMind开发出AlphaGo时，开源版本Leela很快应运而生。卡尔森、法比亚诺等顶级棋手正是与Leela深度融合、理解其策略并模仿其招式的先锋。  

（01:28:06）所以，我认为关键在于尽可能提升自己的综合能力。同时，保持适当的休息也很重要，这不仅有助于心理健康，更能让思路更清晰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Excellent advice. And with that, Nabeel, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 非常棒的建议。好的，纳比尔，我们现在要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here we go. What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。你最常向他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: The first one that comes to mind is Impro by Keith Johnstone. This is actually ... I wrote about it in that essay. It's one of the books that [inaudible 01:28:36] used to send to people. I just think it's a really interesting book. So nominally speaking, it's about improvisational theater, which I believe this guy was a pioneer of. He was a British guy, Keith Johnstone, active between the '60s and the 80s I think. And Impro is just this really interesting book about creativity and how social behavior works and basically just what he taught his improv students. It's a very weird book. It's full of these unbelievably strange ideas. There's a lot of very tactical things he tells you to do in the first chapter, for example, just to break out of your own mental frameworks, really just wild stuff. (01:29:16): He'll tell you to walk backwards while counting down from a hundred and think about some problem that you're struggling with and there's all these kind of odd things. But the number of ideas per page I've found on that book is extremely high. The concepts about how social interaction works and how things like status and so on play into your social behavior are super important. And they made every kind of fully deployed engineer read that for the simple reason that I think it just helps you kind of read people better and interact with them better and become more conscious of how you are coming across and just modulate that.
turns.zh: 首先想到的是基思·约翰斯通的《即兴》。这本书实际上……我在那篇文章里写过。这本书是我过去常推荐给别人的。我觉得它非常有趣。严格来说，这本书讲的是即兴戏剧，我相信这位先驱者是英国人，名字叫基思·约翰斯通，活跃于60到80年代。《即兴》这本书探讨了创造力和社会行为机制，基本上就是他教给学生的东西。这本书非常奇特，里面有很多令人难以置信的奇思妙想。第一章就有很多实用技巧，比如打破思维框架，非常疯狂的建议。（01:29:16）他会让你倒着走路，从100倒数，同时思考自己正在纠结的问题，还有各种奇怪的练习。但每页书中提出的观点密度极高，那些关于社会互动机制、地位等因素如何影响行为的概念非常重要。每个工程师都应该读一读这本书，原因很简单，它能帮助你更好地理解他人，更有效地与人沟通，并更清楚自己的言行给别人的印象，从而进行调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the title again?
turns.zh: 标题再说一遍是什么？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Impro.
turns.zh: 改进一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Impro. Okay, cool. We'll link into it in the show notes.
turns.zh: 再改进一下。好的，太棒了。我们会在节目笔记里提到这个的。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yeah, so Impro is number one. I think just to go a little more highbrow, maybe Shakespeare's history plays, there's a set of them called the Henriad, so like Henry IV, Henry V, Henry VI. I find most people don't read these, so they'll read Hamlet or Macbeth or whatever, but the Henry one is absolutely incredible. You don't have to be interested in British monarchy or British history in order to enjoy them. They're actually some of the most interesting and insightful books I've read about power and how power works and politics and what the sacrifices that you might have to make if you want to be a successful king in that case. But it transfers over. (01:30:35): I think it is worth thinking really hard about, I think especially in a world where everything is kind of organized around these prominent figures and personalities now. When you think about the current administration, you think Trump, Elon, or when you think about AI, you think of Sam Dario, right? And so I think it's important to understand, how do you think about these personalities and yeah, the kind of game that they're playing. And Henry is actually ... the Henriad is an incredible kind of set of books around that. (01:31:05): They're also easy to read, which sounds hilarious when I say it, but you can read a Shakespeare play in a day. They're sort of ... I don't know, they're like 50 pages long. It's not that bad. You have to get used to the language. Yes. But I would recommend that for sure. I guess you asked for two to three. I love High Output Management by Andy Grove. I just think that's a great business book, and people tend to read summaries of it on the internet more than they actually read the book. But the actual book has a lot of really interesting stories and explanations about ... I think the most powerful thing about that book is actually how Andy Grove thinks, and less any of the specific tactics there. And I think you don't get that unless you read how he came up with all these things.
turns.zh: 是的，Impro 排第一。我觉得再说得高深一点，比如莎士比亚的历史剧系列，叫亨利亚德（Henriad），包括《亨利四世》《亨利五世》《亨利六世》。我发现大多数人不读这些剧本，他们会读《哈姆雷特》《麦克白》之类的，但亨利亚德系列绝对令人惊叹。你不必对英国王室或英国历史感兴趣，也能从中获得乐趣。这些书实际上是我读过的最有趣、最具洞察力的作品之一，涉及权力运作、政治博弈，以及为了成为成功的君王可能必须做出的牺牲。但其中的道理是共通的。（01:30:35）我认为这值得深思，尤其是在当今世界，一切似乎都围绕着这些杰出人物和名人展开。当你想到现政府时，想到特朗普、埃隆·马斯克；谈到人工智能时，想到山姆·达里奥，对吧？所以我认为理解这些人物及其玩的游戏很重要。亨利亚德系列确实……是一套令人惊叹的书籍。（01:31:05）它们也很容易阅读，说起来有点好笑，但你一天就能读完一部莎士比亚戏剧。它们大概……50页左右，不算太难。你得适应那种语言。是的。但我肯定会推荐这两本。安迪·格鲁夫的《高效能人士的七个习惯》。我觉得这是一本很棒的商业书籍，人们更多是在网上看总结而不是真正读这本书。但原著里有很多有趣的故事和解释……我认为这本书最有价值的地方在于安迪·格鲁夫的思维方式，而不是书中提到的具体策略。除非你了解他是如何想出所有这些策略的，否则你无法领会其中的精髓。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your first two books were extremely out there versus what other people have recommended, and the third book was the most recommended book on this podcast. So I love that spectrum that we just went on. Perfect. Okay, next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've just really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你推荐的前两本书和其他人推荐的书差别很大，而第三本书是这个播客上被推荐最多的书。所以我很喜欢我们刚刚讨论的这种多样性。太棒了。好的，下一个问题。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: The last movie I really loved was a Decision to Leave. It's a Korean movie. It's by the Director of Old Boy, which maybe some people have heard of. It's a great movie. I think it was released a couple years ago and the basic premise is, there's a detective who is investigating a woman who's accused of killing her husband, and he gradually starts falling for her, which starts to affect his judgment in all these ways. Just a really fascinating kind of psychological thriller with a sort of romantic element to it. Visually, very beautiful. Yeah, I think a lot of the most interesting movies nowadays come from abroad actually. So East Asia, South Asia, places like that. TV, I don't watch so much yet. It's been a while.
turns.zh: 我最近特别喜欢的一部电影是《离家》。是韩国电影，由《老男孩》的导演执导，可能有些人听说过。这是一部很棒的电影。它是几年前上映的，基本剧情是，侦探调查一名被指控杀害丈夫的女性，但逐渐对她产生感情，进而影响了他的判断。这是一部非常引人入胜的心理惊悚片，还带有浪漫元素。视觉效果也非常美。是的，我觉得现在很多最有趣的电影都来自国外。比如东亚、南亚之类的地方。电视剧的话，我最近没怎么看了。已经有一阵子了。

turns.en: Totally understandable for a founder. Okay, next question. Do you have a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you just really love? It could be an app, it could be something physical, it could be a water bottle.
turns.zh: 完全可以理解，作为创始人这很正常。好的，下一个问题。你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？可能是应用，也可能是实体商品，比如水杯之类的。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: I don't have a good answer to that one. I guess I don't buy enough stuff.
turns.zh: 这个问题我答不上来。我觉得我买的东西太少了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fully acceptable. There's no wrong answers in the lightning round. Moving on, do you have a favorite life motto that you often find useful in work or in life that you come back to, that you share with friends or family?
turns.zh: 完全没关系。闪电问答环节没有正确答案。接下来，你有没有最喜欢的的人生格言？那种在工作或生活中常用的、反复回味、与朋友或家人分享的？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: So there's this architect called Christopher Alexander who wrote these beautiful books that are about beauty and kind of more than architecture. And he was a teacher at UC, Berkeley, and he got really frustrated with the students because he just felt like they were always turning in kind of average work. And so he would always tell them every week, imagine there's a gothic cathedral in France called Charge. And he would say, you have to aim for Charge. You have to make something that is better than that. That should be your goal, not to just turn in something that's what you feel is good enough. You actually have to try and be better than the very, very best that ever did it. And I find myself just repeating this a lot to myself. It's just aim for that, really try and do that. Otherwise, it's very easy to anchor on something right in the middle. And you do this unconsciously all the time.
turns.zh: 有个叫克里斯托弗·亚历山大的建筑师，他写过几本关于美的书，内容远不止建筑。他曾在加州大学伯克利分校任教，但对学生很失望，因为总觉得他们的作业平庸。他每周都会给学生讲，假设法国有座叫尚蒂伊的哥特式大教堂。你必须以尚蒂伊为目标，创作出超越它的作品。这才是你的目标，而不是仅仅满足于自己觉得足够好的作品。你必须超越前人。我经常默默对自己说这句话。永远朝着那个目标努力，否则很容易陷入平庸。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So is that the motto, just aim for Charge?
turns.zh: 那这就是你的格言？就是以尚蒂伊为目标？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Most people have no idea what that would be, but with the context is quite powerful. Final question, what's a classic novel that `you think would be most valuable for product builders?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。大多数人可能不知道这是指什么，但结合上下文就很有力量。最后一个问题，哪本经典小说对产品开发者最有价值？

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: My favorite novel is Anna Karenina, and I would recommend that everyone read Erica.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的书是《安娜·卡列尼娜》，还推荐大家读《艾丽卡》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm reading that right now. I've never read it before.
turns.zh: 我现在正在读这本书，以前从没读过。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: No way. And yeah, so it's by Leo Tolstoy. It's this epic 19th century Russian novel that follows a set of characters across society. And I think it's just extraordinary because what's amazing about him is he's just able to imagine himself into the brain of anybody. And so even ... he will briefly just go into the consciousness of, I don't know, the servant who's bringing the meal to the table or something like that. And he'll just tell you a page of what they were thinking, and then he'll just flip back into his main character's head. And I think that is the most impressive demonstration of this kind of skill I've ever seen. (01:35:12): And I think, to connect it to your question, this is what you have to do if you're going to be really good at product, is you have to really think yourself into the other person's head, and you have to be really seeing it the way that they do. And it's so hard, especially as a founder or product person, not to just get stuck on your own way of seeing the problem, right? You wrote up this doc, you made these marks. You're like, this is going to be great. And then you take it to somebody, they don't care that much. You really have to exercise your empathy and understand why they see it that way and what they actually care about.
turns.zh: 不会吧。他是列夫·托尔斯泰的作品。这部19世纪俄罗斯史诗级小说，追踪了社会各阶层人物的命运。我觉得它太伟大了，托尔斯泰能设身处地地从任何人的视角出发。比如他会短暂进入仆人端饭的意识流，描述他们的想法，再切换回主角视角。这是我见过最令人惊叹的叙事技巧。（01:35:12）这和你的问题有关——要想做好产品，就必须真正设身处地为他人着想，理解他们的视角。这对创始人或产品经理来说尤其重要，别总局限于自己的视角。写好文档，标注需求后，对方却不感兴趣。这时你就需要锻炼同理心，理解对方的关切所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a beautiful way to bring it all together. Let me also add, while I'm reading the book, something ... a tip here is, people talk about having Chat GPT voice mode, just kind of sitting there next to you. I found that extremely helpful with this book where I just ask what the hell does this thing mean? There's all these Russian dances and balls and etiquette. You just ask and you're like, I'm reading Anna Karenina, what does this mean? And it just tells you.
turns.zh: 把所有内容整合起来的方式真是太棒了。还要补充一点，我在读这本书的时候，发现有个小技巧……比如，人们常说Chat GPT有语音模式，就好像它坐在你旁边一样。我发现这对读《安娜·卡列尼娜》特别有用——当我遇到不理解的地方，比如俄罗斯的舞会礼仪之类的，只要问一句“这到底什么意思？”它就能立刻给出解释。

turns.speaker: Nabeel S. Qureshi
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。
